posts.title: Razor-thin 50.96% to 49.04% split. Boyenga took Atwater, McSwain in early mail. # #mercedcounty #usa
posts.caption:
715 votes. That is the entire spread separating Ana Boyenga (19,012) and Richard Lopez (18,297) with 37,309 votes logged so far.  

The green and blue map looks dramatic, but here is what the establishment isn't telling you: this board is still running off Batch 1.  

Batch 1 consists primarily of early vote-by-mail ballots returned weeks ago, which historically lean older and more conservative.  

What hasn’t hit the board yet?
Thousands of ballots dropped into county drop boxes on Tuesday.  

Postmarked mail arriving throughout the week.

Provisional and same-day registration ballots (currently sitting at zero).  

In Merced County, that late count heavily represents working families and the Latino vote.  

Boyenga took Atwater, McSwain, and Buhach on early mail, but the race is sitting on a razor-thin 50.96% to 49.04% split.  

Do not call this race early. The canvass has only just started.

Drop your thoughts below: Did you vote early, or did you hit the drop box on Tuesday? 🗳️

posts.title: A Sanctuary Law Is Only As Strong As Its Warrant | Salem, Oregon ICE Detentions
posts.caption:
Central Valley governance. Merced County spending. Administrative accountability.
This is a systems story, not just a Salem story. Oregon's sanctuary promise draws a clear line: no city property for immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant. On October 9th, federal agents entered a closed construction site at McKay Park and detained three workers. The city says it had no advance notice, and when asked whether agents carried a warrant, Homeland Security did not answer. The next day brought tear gas on Lancaster Drive: at least 30 people hit. Advocates count 21 Oregonians detained in three days. Here is the systems question: a sanctuary law is only as strong as its enforcement mechanism. If federal agents can enter closed city property, detain workers, and decline to show paper, then the promise is just a press release. Thirty residents physically blocked agents once. The city is now demanding answers on the record. Watch whether the warrant question gets an answer, because that answer tells you whether the system works.
I run the 209 Audit: public records, receipts, and accountability across Merced County. Full breakdowns every Tuesday in the 209connect newsletter.
